column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.4

column3: Which oblique abdominal layer lies directly beneath external oblique?
column4: Internal oblique.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.4

column3: Which oblique abdominal muscle is closest to the skin?
column4: External oblique.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.4

column3: Which longitudinal muscle group runs on either side of the vertebral column?
column4: Erector spinae.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.3

column3: Which large superficial buttock muscle lies behind the hip?
column4: Gluteus maximus.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: What collective name refers to iliacus and psoas major?
column4: Iliopsoas.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which four-muscle group occupies the anterior thigh?
column4: Quadriceps femoris.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: What collective name covers semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris?
column4: Hamstrings.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which functional muscle group occupies much of the medial thigh?
column4: Hip adductors.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Gluteus medius and minimus belong to which functional group at the hip?
column4: Hip abductors.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which anterior shin muscle attaches on the medial side of the foot?
column4: Tibialis anterior.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which large calf muscle lies deep to gastrocnemius and does not cross the knee?
column4: Soleus.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which superficial two-headed calf muscle originates on the femur?
column4: Gastrocnemius.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: What is the anatomical name for the collarbone?
column4: Clavicle.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.1

column3: Which shoulder-girdle bone articulates directly with the sternum?
column4: Clavicle.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.1

column3: What is the anatomical name for the shoulder blade?
column4: Scapula.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.1

column3: Which socket of the scapula receives the head of the humerus?
column4: Glenoid cavity.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.1

column3: What is the anatomical name for the breastbone?
column4: Sternum.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §7.4

column3: What palpable inferior tip of the sternum should be distinguished from the main body?
column4: Xiphoid process.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §7.4

column3: What is the anatomical name for the upper arm bone?
column4: Humerus.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: Which end of the humerus meets the scapula?
column4: The proximal end (humeral head).
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: What is the anatomical name for the cluster of eight wrist bones?
column4: Carpals.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: How are the carpal bones arranged in each wrist?
column4: Two rows of four.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: What is the anatomical name for the forearm bone on the little-finger side?
column4: Ulna.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: Which part of the ulna forms the point of the elbow?
column4: Olecranon.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: What is the anatomical name for the forearm bone on the thumb side?
column4: Radius.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: Which forearm bone crosses over the other during pronation?
column4: The radius crosses the ulna.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.2

column3: What is the anatomical name for the thigh bone?
column4: Femur.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: Which socket receives the femoral head?
column4: Acetabulum.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: What is the anatomical name for the slender lateral lower-leg bone?
column4: Fibula.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: Which bone forms the lateral malleolus at the ankle?
column4: Fibula.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: What is the anatomical name for the large medial shin bone?
column4: Tibia.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: Which lower-leg bone bears most of the weight transferred from the femur?
column4: Tibia.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: What is the anatomical name for the group of seven proximal foot bones?
column4: Tarsals.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: Which tarsal bone forms the heel?
column4: Calcaneus.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §8.4

column3: Which plane contains a standing cable hip adduction performed directly sideways?
column4: Frontal.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6; §§9.5, 10.4

column3: A client bends and straightens the knee in a seated leg extension. Which anatomical plane contains the main joint motion?
column4: Sagittal.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: What anatomical plane divides the body into front and back portions?
column4: Frontal (coronal).
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §1.6 Anatomical Terminology, Planes of the Body.

column3: A standing torso turn occurs mainly in which plane?
column4: Transverse (horizontal).
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: What matters about the vertical line through the center of gravity during quiet standing?
column4: Its projection must remain within the base of support for static equilibrium without external assistance.
column5: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, §9.3 Stability; Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§7.3, 10.4 and 10.6

column3: What change to foot spacing generally increases side-to-side stability on level ground?
column4: Widen the stance to increase the base of support.
column5: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, §9.3 Stability; Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§7.3, 10.4 and 10.6

column3: All else equal, how does lowering the center of gravity affect resistance to tipping?
column4: It increases stability.
column5: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, §9.3 Stability; Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§7.3, 10.4 and 10.6

column3: What is meant by a neutral spine during a loaded hinge?
column4: Maintain the spine's natural curves while motion occurs primarily at the hips.
column5: OpenStax, College Physics 2e, §9.3 Stability; Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§7.3, 10.4 and 10.6

column3: An exaggerated inward lumbar curve is called what?
column4: Excessive lumbar lordosis. Some lumbar lordosis is normal.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: What term describes an abnormal lateral spinal curvature, often accompanied by vertebral rotation?
column4: Scoliosis.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: What term describes the normally posteriorly convex thoracic curve?
column4: Kyphosis. Excessive curvature is hyperkyphosis.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: Which synovial joint type primarily permits flexion and extension about one axis?
column4: Hinge.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: What joint shape lets the shoulder move around multiple axes?
column4: Ball-and-socket.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: What type of synovial joint permits the atlas to rotate around the dens?
column4: Pivot.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: Which joint type allows opposition at the base of the thumb?
column4: Saddle.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: What do the middle fibers of the trapezius do to the scapula?
column4: Retract it toward the spine.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.5

column3: What action of pectoralis major brings a raised upper arm across the chest?
column4: Horizontal adduction at the shoulder.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.5

column3: What shoulder action does latissimus dorsi produce when pulling the upper arm backward?
column4: Extension.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.5

column3: Which shoulder action is the middle deltoid best positioned to produce?
column4: Abduction.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.5

column3: Besides flexing the elbow, how does biceps brachii turn the forearm?
column4: It supinates it.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.5

column3: What elbow action does the triceps produce?
column4: Extension.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.5

column3: How does rectus abdominis move the trunk in a curl-up?
column4: It flexes the trunk.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.4

column3: Toward which side does one internal oblique rotate the trunk?
column4: Toward the same side.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.4

column3: Toward which side does one external oblique rotate the trunk?
column4: Toward the opposite side.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.4

column3: What spinal movement occurs when the erector spinae on both sides shorten to straighten a flexed trunk?
column4: Spinal extension.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.3

column3: What is the main hip action of gluteus maximus when rising from a chair?
column4: Hip extension.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Lifting the thigh forward recruits iliopsoas for which action?
column4: Hip flexion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which knee motion is shared by all four quadriceps muscles?
column4: Extension.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: What knee action is common to the hamstrings?
column4: Flexion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Why can the long head of biceps femoris act at both hip and knee?
column4: It crosses both joints.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6; §§9.5, 10.4

column3: What movement do hip adductors produce when squeezing a ball between the thighs?
column4: Hip adduction, or an adduction force if the ball prevents motion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which action moves the thigh sideways using gluteus medius?
column4: Hip abduction.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: What ankle movement does tibialis anterior produce when lifting the forefoot?
column4: Dorsiflexion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Which ankle motion can soleus generate with the knee bent?
column4: Plantar flexion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: Why does bending the knee shorten gastrocnemius without directly shortening soleus at its origin?
column4: Only gastrocnemius crosses the knee.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6; §§9.5, 10.4

column3: Besides plantar flexion, which knee action can gastrocnemius assist?
column4: Flexion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §11.6

column3: What does joint range of motion measure?
column4: The excursion available at a joint, commonly expressed in degrees.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§1.6, 7.3, 9.4–9.6

column3: During a goniometric elbow-flexion assessment, which magnitude is closer to the CDC study mean for healthy adults aged 20–44: 90° or 145–150°?
column4: About 145–150°. These are group means, not requirements for an individual.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: To describe hamstring-driven knee flexion, is 0° normally the starting straight-knee position or full heel-to-buttock flexion?
column4: The straight-knee position. Flexion increases the angle recorded from anatomical zero.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: Which active ankle excursion should be assessed if a client has difficulty lifting the forefoot toward the shin?
column4: Dorsiflexion from neutral.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: A client points the foot away from the shin to demonstrate calf-driven range. Which arc is being measured?
column4: Ankle plantar flexion.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: Which has the larger typical excursion from neutral in the CDC adult reference data, hip flexion or hip extension?
column4: Hip flexion. Flexion exceeds 120° on average, while extension averages under 20° in ages 20–44.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: A trainer measures forward overhead reach with the rib cage kept still. Which shoulder movement is being assessed?
column4: Shoulder flexion.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: What compensation could falsely increase apparent hip abduction range during a standing side lift?
column4: Pelvic hiking or trunk leaning substitutes for motion at the hip.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: Why should scapular motion be observed when assessing overhead arm elevation?
column4: Full overhead elevation combines glenohumeral movement with scapular upward rotation.
column5: CDC, Normal Joint Range of Motion Study, Reference Values for Normal Joint Range of Motion, ages 20–44; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5–9.6 and 11.5–11.6 Open source

column3: A client sits with the arm raised in front and opens it sideways at shoulder height. Which shoulder excursion lengthens the pectoralis major across the chest?
column4: Horizontal abduction.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5 and 11.3–11.6; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology

column3: From anatomical position, a client reaches forward and overhead in the sagittal plane with the lower ribs held still. Which shoulder excursion lengthens latissimus dorsi?
column4: Shoulder flexion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5 and 11.3–11.6; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology

column3: Why does an overhead triceps stretch combine elbow flexion with shoulder elevation?
column4: The long head crosses both joints; this combination lengthens it across both.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5 and 11.3–11.6; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology

column3: A client uncurls the trunk from flexion back to neutral. What happens to rectus abdominis length through that excursion?
column4: It lengthens as the spine extends toward neutral.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5 and 11.3–11.6; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology

column3: A seated client turns the ribs right while the pelvis follows. How can a trainer isolate the trunk rotation produced by the obliques?
column4: Stabilize or monitor the pelvis and measure rib-cage rotation relative to it.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5 and 11.3–11.6; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology

column3: Which excursion lengthens the spinal extensors when the pelvis is held steady?
column4: Spinal flexion.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5 and 11.3–11.6; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology

column3: Which energy pathway uses oxygen and can sustain ATP production over long efforts?
column4: Aerobic metabolism, primarily mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: Which stored compound rapidly replenishes ATP at the start of a maximal jump?
column4: Creatine phosphate.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: Which pathway quickly supplies ATP from glucose without directly consuming oxygen?
column4: Glycolysis.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: Do the energy systems switch on one at a time during a sprint?
column4: No. All contribute, with their relative contributions changing over the effort.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: What mitochondrial adaptation helps trained muscle sustain oxidative ATP production?
column4: Greater mitochondrial content and oxidative capacity.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: What normally happens to cardiac output during graded dynamic exercise?
column4: It rises to deliver more blood to active tissues.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: What two variables determine cardiac output?
column4: Heart rate and stroke volume multiplied together.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: At 150 beats/min and 100 mL/beat, what is cardiac output in L/min?
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: During a heavy sustained contraction, what can occur to blood flow through the contracting muscle?
column4: Mechanical compression can transiently restrict flow.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: What structural muscle change can support long-term gains in force after resistance training?
column4: Increased muscle fiber cross-sectional area.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: How can continued light movement in a cool-down support venous return?
column4: Contracting leg muscles keep the skeletal-muscle pump active.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: Why start a session with progressively easier-to-harder movement?
column4: A gradual warm-up increases muscle temperature and circulatory demand progressively.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: How does acute muscle fatigue affect force during a set?
column4: The capacity to produce the required force declines during or immediately after activity.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: Which type of unfamiliar muscle loading is especially associated with delayed-onset soreness?
column4: Eccentric loading.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: A client feels sudden focal pain and loses function mid-repetition. Is delayed-onset muscle soreness the likely explanation?
column4: No. Stop and assess for injury; DOMS develops later.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: Which mismatch underlies an overtraining syndrome concern?
column4: Persistent overload relative to recovery, with prolonged performance decline after other causes are considered.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: Why can an endurance-trained client maintain resting cardiac output with fewer beats per minute?
column4: A larger stroke volume can offset a lower heart rate.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: After aerobic conditioning, how does heart rate typically change at the same absolute submaximal cycling workload?
column4: It decreases.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: Which rises more with aerobic training in most adults, maximal heart rate or maximal stroke volume?
column4: Maximal stroke volume.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: How does endurance training typically affect oxygen extraction by active muscle?
column4: It can increase extraction through peripheral oxidative and capillary adaptations.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: What performance adaptation is expected after repeated high-intensity anaerobic training?
column4: Improved capacity to generate or sustain high power in brief efforts.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: What can explain early gains in lifting strength before substantial muscle enlargement?
column4: Improved neural activation and coordination.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: Which fiber profile favors sustained, repeated low-force contractions?
column4: Slow oxidative fibers, rich in mitochondria and resistant to fatigue.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: On standing suddenly, what immediate mechanical change can briefly lower blood pressure?
column4: Gravity pools blood in the lower body and reduces venous return.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: What usually happens to systolic pressure as dynamic exercise intensity rises?
column4: It rises as cardiac output increases.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§19.4, 20.2–20.4

column3: What resting BP trend is common with regular aerobic training, particularly with elevated baseline BP?
column4: A reduction in resting blood pressure.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: What term describes an increase in the size of existing muscle fibers?
column4: Hypertrophy.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: What process reduces fiber size during prolonged disuse?
column4: Atrophy.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: What distinguishes hyperplasia from hypertrophy?
column4: Hyperplasia increases cell number.
column5: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§10.3–10.6

column3: What is dynapenia?
column4: Loss of muscular strength with aging, which may exceed the change in muscle mass.
column5: Clark & Manini, What is dynapenia?, Nutrition 2012, Definition of dynapenia (PMID 22469152).

column3: Which finding prompts suspicion of sarcopenia under EWGSOP2?
column4: Low muscle strength. Low muscle quantity or quality confirms the diagnosis clinically.
column5: EWGSOP2, Sarcopenia: revised European consensus on definition and diagnosis, Defining Sarcopenia; ESPEN/EASO Consensus, Definition and Diagnostic Criteria for Sarcopenic Obesity

column3: What combination defines sarcopenic obesity?
column4: Excess adiposity together with low muscle mass and impaired muscle function.
column5: EWGSOP2, Sarcopenia: revised European consensus on definition and diagnosis, Defining Sarcopenia; ESPEN/EASO Consensus, Definition and Diagnostic Criteria for Sarcopenic Obesity

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does cardiovascular endurance describe?
column4: How well the heart, lungs and muscles support sustained rhythmic work.
column5: ATS, Guidelines for the Six-Minute Walk Test, sections Indications and Interpretation Open source

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does body composition describe?
column4: The relative amounts of fat and fat-free tissue.
column5: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12e (GETP12), chapter Health-Related Physical Fitness Testing and Interpretation, Body Composition

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does muscular strength describe?
column4: The greatest force a muscle group can produce in one effort.
column5: GETP12, Health-Related Physical Fitness Testing and Interpretation, Muscular Fitness

column3: What distinguishes muscular endurance from maximal strength?
column4: Muscular endurance is the ability to sustain or repeat submaximal force over time.
column5: GETP12, Health-Related Physical Fitness Testing and Interpretation, Muscular Fitness

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does flexibility describe?
column4: Available range of movement at a joint or series of joints.
column5: GETP12, Health-Related Physical Fitness Testing and Interpretation, Flexibility

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does agility describe?
column4: The ability to change speed or direction effectively in response to a stimulus.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, chapters 13 and 19

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does coordination describe?
column4: The ability to organize sensory input and body movements into a smooth accurate action.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 12 Client Fitness Assessments; ACE, 5 Winter Activities for Kids, The Impossible Card Catch (hand–eye coordination).

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does balance describe?
column4: Control of body position over the base of support.
column5: CDC STEADI, The 4-Stage Balance Test, instructions and interpretation

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does power describe?
column4: The rate of doing mechanical work.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 13, Maximum Muscular Power

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does reaction time describe?
column4: The interval from a stimulus to the start of a response.
column5: Schmidt et al., Motor Control and Learning, 6e, Information Processing and Decision Making

column3: In a fitness assessment, what does speed describe?
column4: The ability to cover distance in a short time.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, chapters 13 and 19

column3: Which two broad physiological factors determine maximal oxygen uptake under the Fick principle?
column4: Maximal cardiac output and the arteriovenous oxygen difference.

column4: Slow, controlled weight shifts and coordinated changes of stance.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 16.

column4: Walking.

column4: Alternate brief jogs with walking recovery and progress gradually.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 4, Key Guidelines for Adults and Explaining the Guidelines Open source

column4: Impact loading at landing.

column4: Stationary cycling.

column4: 150–300 minutes per week.

column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 4, Key Guidelines for Adults and Explaining the Guidelines Open source

column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 4, Key Guidelines for Adults and Explaining the Guidelines Open source

column4: At least 2 days per week.

column3: How should movement be distributed for preschool-age children ages 3–5?

column3: What daily activity duration is recommended for ages 6–17?
column4: At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity each day.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3, Key Guidelines for Preschool-Aged Children and School-Aged Children and Adolescents Open source

column3: How much of the school-age child's daily activity should be aerobic?
column4: Most of it.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3, Key Guidelines for Preschool-Aged Children and School-Aged Children and Adolescents Open source

column3: How often should vigorous aerobic activity be included for ages 6–17?
column4: At least 3 days per week.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3, Key Guidelines for Preschool-Aged Children and School-Aged Children and Adolescents Open source

column3: How often should school-age youth include bone-strengthening activity?
column4: At least 3 days per week as part of their daily activity.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3, Key Guidelines for Preschool-Aged Children and School-Aged Children and Adolescents Open source

column3: How often should adolescents include muscle-strengthening activity?
column4: At least 3 days per week as part of daily activity.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3, Key Guidelines for Preschool-Aged Children and School-Aged Children and Adolescents Open source

column3: What component should older adults add to aerobic and strengthening activity in a multicomponent program?
column4: Balance training.

column3: For generally healthy pregnant clients without contraindications, what weekly amount of moderate aerobic activity is recommended?
column4: At least 150 minutes spread throughout the week.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 6, Women During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period; ACOG Committee Opinion 804, Box 3 and Recommendations Open source

column3: Why use relative effort to guide aerobic activity during pregnancy?
column4: Physiologic changes and individual fitness affect the response to a given workload.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 6, Women During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period; ACOG Committee Opinion 804, Box 3 and Recommendations Open source

column3: Why is stationary cycling often preferable to outdoor cycling as pregnancy changes balance?
column4: It reduces fall risk while preserving an aerobic option.
column5: ACOG, Exercise During Pregnancy FAQ, Precautions, Activities to Avoid and Warning Signs Open source

column3: Does a school-age child's muscle-strengthening activity require weight machines?
column4: No. Climbing or other play that overloads muscles can count.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3–6, age-specific key guidelines and explaining the guidelines Open source

column3: A teen's 60 minutes already include ten minutes of jumping. Must bone-strengthening minutes be added on top of the 60?
column4: No. They can be part of the daily total.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3–6, age-specific key guidelines and explaining the guidelines Open source

column3: Does walking alone reliably provide every component recommended for older adults?
column4: No. Include muscle-strengthening and balance work as well.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 3–6, age-specific key guidelines and explaining the guidelines Open source

column3: In FITT, which variable changes if a client adds a fourth training day but keeps each session the same?
column4: Frequency.

column4: Intensity.

column4: Type.

column4: Volume.

column3: Why should a client using insulin coordinate exercise timing and glucose monitoring with their diabetes plan?
column4: Exercise can increase glucose use and hypoglycemia risk during or after the session.

column3: For a client on hemodialysis who wants a new workout immediately after dialysis, what timing adjustment does ACSM EIM advise?

column3: A cleared client has an arm dialysis fistula. What pressure precaution applies when selecting resistance exercises?
column4: Avoid placing direct weight or pressure on the fistula.

column3: A client with diabetes and reduced foot sensation plans a new walking program. What should be monitored alongside exercise dose?

column3: Why use RPE along with the clinical prescription when a heart medication blunts exercise heart rate?

column3: For a cleared adult with stable CKD, what aerobic frequency does ACSM's EIM handout suggest as tolerated?

column5: ACSM Exercise is Medicine, Being Active When You Have Chronic Kidney Disease, Aerobic Activity and Strength Training Open source

column4: 2–3 days per week with a rest day between.
column5: ACSM Exercise is Medicine, Being Active When You Have Chronic Kidney Disease, Aerobic Activity and Strength Training Open source

column4: 2–3 sessions per week on nonconsecutive days.

column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology and ch. 4 Biomechanics; OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5, 11.5–11.6

column4: Plantar flexion. The forefoot stays in contact as the heel rises.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 3 Anatomy and Kinesiology and ch. 4 Biomechanics; OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, §§9.5, 11.5–11.6

column3: A walker can speak in sentences but cannot sing comfortably. What relative aerobic intensity does the talk test suggest?
column4: Moderate.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 4, Key Guidelines for Adults and Explaining the Guidelines Open source

column3: During an effort a client can say only a few words before pausing for breath. What intensity does that suggest?
column4: Vigorous relative intensity.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 4, Key Guidelines for Adults and Explaining the Guidelines Open source

column3: What is the difference between an absolute MET level and relative intensity?
column4: METs describe energy cost. Relative intensity expresses demand compared with the individual's capacity.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 4, Key Guidelines for Adults and Explaining the Guidelines Open source

column3: What oxygen consumption is conventionally assigned to 1 MET?
column4: 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: A task requires 21 mL O₂/kg/min. What is its estimated MET level?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: At 70 kg, a measured oxygen uptake of 2.1 L/min equals what relative oxygen uptake?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: At 5 METs for 40 minutes, how many MET-minutes does a client accumulate?
column4: 200 MET-minutes. 5 × 40 = 200.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: What absolute MET range defines moderate-intensity activity for adults?
column4: 3.0 to less than 6.0 METs.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: At what absolute intensity does vigorous adult activity begin in METs?
column4: 6 METs.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: A client covers 3 km in 24 minutes. What is the average pace?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: A treadmill is set to 6 km/h. How many minutes per kilometer is that?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: A trainer counts 32 beats over a stable 15-second interval. What is the estimated heart rate?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: What is oxygen uptake reserve?
column4: Maximal oxygen uptake minus resting oxygen uptake.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: VO₂max is 43.5 and resting VO₂ is 3.5 mL/kg/min. What target is 50% VO₂ reserve?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: What does a whole-body rating of perceived exertion capture?
column4: The client's overall sense of how hard the effort feels.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: On the Borg 6–20 scale, what range generally corresponds to moderate aerobic intensity?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, FITT-VP, Cardiorespiratory Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; Garber et al., ACSM Position Stand, Recommendations for Exercise Prescription, flexibility and neuromotor sections

column3: An activity costs 4 METs for two clients. Why might only one experience vigorous relative effort?
column4: The same absolute energy cost uses a larger fraction of capacity in the less fit client.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, FITT-VP, Cardiorespiratory Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; Garber et al., ACSM Position Stand, Recommendations for Exercise Prescription, flexibility and neuromotor sections

column3: At a steady 8 min/km pace, how far will a client travel in a 36-minute work bout?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, FITT-VP, Cardiorespiratory Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; Garber et al., ACSM Position Stand, Recommendations for Exercise Prescription, flexibility and neuromotor sections

column3: A client cycles at 6 METs for 25 minutes on two days. What is the weekly cycling volume in MET-minutes?
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, FITT-VP, Cardiorespiratory Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; Garber et al., ACSM Position Stand, Recommendations for Exercise Prescription, flexibility and neuromotor sections

column3: Why must relative oxygen uptake be converted before directly comparing it with a value in L/min?
column4: One is adjusted for body mass; the other is absolute oxygen consumption.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, FITT-VP, Cardiorespiratory Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; Garber et al., ACSM Position Stand, Recommendations for Exercise Prescription, flexibility and neuromotor sections

column3: A wrist device abruptly reports 210 bpm during easy cycling, but the client feels normal. Before using that number to change the training zone, what should the trainer verify?
column4: Reduce or pause the effort and confirm the heart rate with a reliable measurement while assessing symptoms.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 12 Client Fitness Assessments and ch. 15 Cardiorespiratory Training Programs

column3: Does an RPE of 13 on the Borg 6–20 scale mean 13 on a 0–10 effort scale?
column4: No. Confirm the specific scale and its anchors before interpreting the number.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 12 Client Fitness Assessments and ch. 15 Cardiorespiratory Training Programs

column3: Resting HR is 60 bpm and maximal HR is 180 bpm. What target corresponds to 60% HR reserve?
column5: ACSM, Exercising Your Way to Lowering Your Blood Pressure, Intensity — How hard should we push ourselves? (heart-rate calculations). Open source

column3: Resting HR is 70 bpm and maximal HR is 170 bpm. A client exercises at 115 bpm. What percent of HR reserve is this?
column5: ACSM, Exercising Your Way to Lowering Your Blood Pressure, Intensity — How hard should we push ourselves? (heart-rate calculations). Open source

column3: Using the specified estimate HRmax = 220 − age, what is the predicted maximum for a 45-year-old?
column5: ACSM, Exercising Your Way to Lowering Your Blood Pressure, Intensity — How hard should we push ourselves? (heart-rate calculations). Open source

column3: Why can't a trainer simply multiply HRmax by 0.60 to calculate 60% HR reserve?
column4: The reserve method uses the span above rest and adds resting HR back.
column5: ACSM, Exercising Your Way to Lowering Your Blood Pressure, Intensity — How hard should we push ourselves? (heart-rate calculations). Open source

column3: What HR-reserve range represents moderate intensity in the ACSM relative classification?
column4: 40% to less than 60% HRR.
column5: ACSM, Exercising Your Way to Lowering Your Blood Pressure, Intensity — How hard should we push ourselves? (heart-rate calculations). Open source

column3: A client takes a beta blocker and has no valid exercise-test HR target. Why avoid prescribing from age-predicted HRmax alone?
column4: The drug can blunt the HR response. Use appropriate relative exertion measures and clinical guidance.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Table 5.2 and Box 5.2

column3: Using Tanaka's stated equation 208 − 0.7 × age, what is predicted HRmax at age 40?
column5: Tanaka, Monahan & Seals, Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited, JACC 2001, Results (doi:10.1016/S0735-1097(00)01054-8).

column3: Why should an age-predicted maximum be treated as an estimate for an individual client?
column4: Prediction equations have individual error even when the average prediction is reasonable.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, FITT-VP, Cardiorespiratory Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; Garber et al., ACSM Position Stand, Recommendations for Exercise Prescription, flexibility and neuromotor sections

column3: Rest HR is 64 and measured max HR is 164 bpm. What are the 40% and 59% HRR target boundaries?
column5: ACSM, Exercising Your Way to Lowering Your Blood Pressure, Intensity — How hard should we push ourselves? (heart-rate calculations). Open source

column3: A runner's plan alternates higher-volume base weeks with a lower-volume race-specific phase. What planning principle does this illustrate?
column4: Aerobic periodization.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 13.

column3: A strength plan cycles through higher-repetition and heavier low-repetition blocks. Which programming strategy is being used?
column4: Resistance-training periodization.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 13.

column3: A client accumulates fatigue during a demanding conditioning block. How can the next planned block support recovery?
column4: Reduce training volume or intensity temporarily and monitor the response.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 13.

column3: Which planning unit typically represents a short series of sessions such as a training week?
column4: A microcycle.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: What is a mesocycle in a periodized plan?
column4: A training block made of multiple microcycles with a particular emphasis.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: What does a macrocycle encompass?
column4: The longer overall training cycle, often a season or year.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: How does daily undulating programming vary the stimulus?
column4: Load or volume emphasis changes between sessions within a short cycle.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: A runner reduces training volume before a target race while retaining some event-specific intensity. What strategy is this?
column4: A taper.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: What is the purpose of a deload in resistance training?
column4: Temporarily reduce training stress to facilitate recovery.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: ACSM's 2026 healthy-adult guidance favors what loading zone for maximizing strength?
column4: Heavier loads, about 80% 1RM or higher when appropriate.
column5: ACSM 2026 Position Stand, Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults, goal-specific prescription recommendations Open source

column3: What set count per exercise does the 2026 ACSM summary emphasize when optimizing strength?
column4: About 2–3 sets.
column5: ACSM 2026 Position Stand, Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults, goal-specific prescription recommendations Open source

column3: A muscle group gets 3 working sets on Monday, 4 on Wednesday and 3 on Friday. What is the weekly set count?
column5: ACSM 2026 Position Stand, Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults, goal-specific prescription recommendations Open source

column3: What load range does ACSM's 2026 healthy-adult summary give for power-focused resistance work?
column4: About 30–70% of 1RM with fast concentric intent.
column5: ACSM 2026 Position Stand, Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults, goal-specific prescription recommendations Open source

column3: How do endurance-focused sets generally differ in repetition count from near-maximal strength sets?
column4: They use more repetitions with lighter loads.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 14.

column3: Why allow longer recovery during repeated heavy strength or high-power sets?
column4: To preserve force, speed and technique across sets.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 14.

column3: What is the difference between a repetition and a set?
column4: A repetition is one complete exercise cycle. A set is a group of repetitions performed before a rest.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: A client completes 3 sets of 8 reps with 40 kg. What is external volume load?
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: Two workouts have equal volume load. Does that prove identical training stimuli?
column4: No. Load per rep, effort, rest and exercise selection can differ.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: During a power session, jump height drops substantially despite unchanged load. Which between-set variable should be reconsidered first if recovery was shortened?
column4: Rest interval. Restore enough recovery to preserve power.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: A client's tested squat 1RM is 80 kg. What is 75% of that result?
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Training Load and Repetitions.

column3: A client benches 60 kg once with valid technique. What percentage of that 1RM is a 48 kg set?
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Training Load and Repetitions.

column3: A 10RM test yields 35 kg. What does that result mean?
column4: 35 kg is the greatest load lifted ten times with the specified technique under the test conditions.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Training Load and Repetitions.

column3: Can a leg press 1RM be used directly as the squat 1RM when assigning a percentage load?
column4: No. Repetition maxima are exercise- and technique-specific.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Training Load and Repetitions.

column3: What does a lower number in an RM designation imply for the same exercise and client: a lighter or heavier maximal load?
column4: Heavier. A 3RM is heavier than a 10RM under comparable conditions.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 17, Program Design for Resistance Training, and ch. 21, Periodization

column3: How can improved lower-body strength affect daily function in an older adult?
column4: It reduces the fraction of maximum capacity required for tasks such as climbing stairs.
column5: HHS, Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2e, ch. 5, Key Guidelines for Older Adults Open source

column3: Why can the load once used for a difficult set feel easier after strength training?
column4: It represents a smaller fraction of the client's new maximal strength.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 13.

column3: Which adaptation explains smoother execution of a practiced movement without a change in muscle size?
column4: Improved motor coordination.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 13.

column3: Why let a novice practice a movement with minimal resistance before adding substantial load?
column4: It allows learning and assessment of coordination with less fatigue and risk.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 14 Resistance Training Programs

column3: What is the Valsalva maneuver?
column4: A forceful expiratory effort against a closed glottis, raising pressure in the chest and abdomen.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 14.

column3: Why discourage prolonged breath-holding during resistance work in a client with hypertension?
column4: It can cause marked transient blood-pressure fluctuations.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 14.

column3: Why does holding a dumbbell farther from a joint increase the torque demand when force direction is unchanged?
column4: It increases the perpendicular moment arm.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 14, Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training; ch. 15, Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

column3: Why keep a box close to the body during a floor-to-waist lift?
column4: It reduces the external moment arm about the trunk and hips.
column5: NSCA, Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning, 4e, ch. 14, Exercise Technique for Free Weight and Machine Training; ch. 15, Alternative Modes and Nontraditional Implement Training

column3: What distinguishes walking from running in terms of ground contact?
column4: Walking has no flight phase and includes double support.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 17 Personal Training Session Components.

column3: What distinguishes the flight phase of running?
column4: Neither foot contacts the ground.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 17 Personal Training Session Components.

column3: Why does a streamlined swimming position generally make forward movement easier?
column4: It reduces drag from the water.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 17 Personal Training Session Components.

column3: Where does the working foot transmit force to a bicycle's drivetrain?
column4: Through the pedal to the crank.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 17 Personal Training Session Components.

column3: In a standing yoga pose, why can shortening a challenging lever make balance easier?
column4: It can reduce external torque and help keep the center of mass over the base.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 17 Personal Training Session Components.

column3: During a Pilates leg-lowering drill the back starts to arch unintentionally. What change reduces the external lever demand?
column4: Bend the knees or reduce the lowering range while maintaining trunk control.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 17 Personal Training Session Components.

column3: What is the external moment arm of a resistance force about a joint?
column4: The perpendicular distance between the joint axis and the force's line of action.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 14 Resistance Training Programs

column3: A 100 N external force acts with a 0.30 m perpendicular moment arm. What torque does it exert?
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 14 Resistance Training Programs

column3: During an unloaded limb movement, does the absence of a dumbbell eliminate external gravitational torque?
column4: No. The weight of the body segment itself exerts torque.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 14 Resistance Training Programs

column3: Why can a lateral raise with bent elbows be easier than with straight elbows at the same shoulder angle and dumbbell load?
column4: The weight usually lies closer to the shoulder axis, shortening its moment arm.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 14 Resistance Training Programs

column3: Why train carrying a load on one side when the functional goal is carrying a single suitcase?
column4: It challenges resistance to lateral trunk bending under an asymmetric load.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 14 Resistance Training Programs

column3: What is reversibility in exercise training?
column4: Adaptations diminish when the training stimulus is removed or markedly reduced.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 13.

column3: After several inactive months a client struggles with formerly easy stairs. What should determine the restart workload?
column4: Current function and tolerance, reassessed before progression.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 5, General Principles of Exercise Prescription, Cardiorespiratory Exercise, Resistance Exercise, Neuromotor Exercise and Flexibility Exercise; ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 13.

column3: What distinguishes functional overreaching from overtraining syndrome?
column4: The performance decline resolves after short-term recovery and may be followed by improvement.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: A client becomes too exhausted to control technique. What should happen to the current set?
column4: End the set and assess recovery before further work.
column5: ACSM GETP12, chapters 1 and 5, benefits and risks, warm-up, resistance and flexibility exercise; ACSM/ECSS Joint Consensus, Prevention, Diagnosis and Treatment of the Overtraining Syndrome (2013)

column3: A client turns a half squat into a forward fold at the waist. What movement cue restores the intended pattern?
column4: Keep the chest lifted and lower the hips as if sitting back onto a chair.
column5: AAOS OrthoInfo, Knee Conditioning Program, exercises 4–12, Step-by-step directions and Tips Open source

column3: During band external rotation at the side, the elbow drifts away from the ribs. What correction preserves the intended axis?
column4: Keep the elbow bent and near the side as the forearm swings outward.
column5: AAOS OrthoInfo, Rotator Cuff and Shoulder Conditioning Program, Crossover Arm Stretch, Standing Row, Internal Rotation, External Rotation, Elbow Flexion and Scapula Setting Open source

column3: Why should the trainer distinguish hip flexion from lumbar flexion during a hinge?
column4: They occur at different joints, changing load distribution and the intended pattern.
column5: ACSM’s Resources for the Personal Trainer, 6e, ch. 4 Biomechanics and ch. 14 Resistance Training Programs

column3: What is the advantage of removable clothing layers during prolonged cold-weather activity?
column4: Adjust insulation as heat production and weather change while limiting sweat accumulation.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 7, Environmental Considerations for Exercise Prescription, Altitude, Heat, Cold and Air Pollution; EPA, Air Quality Guide for Particle Pollution

column3: Which clothing properties generally help in hot sunny conditions?
column4: Lightweight, loose, light-colored clothing that permits evaporation.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 7, Environmental Considerations for Exercise Prescription, Altitude, Heat, Cold and Air Pollution; EPA, Air Quality Guide for Particle Pollution

column3: Why choose footwear for the intended surface and movement pattern?
column4: Appropriate traction, fit and support help manage slip and loading risks.
column5: ACSM GETP12, ch. 7, Environmental Considerations for Exercise Prescription, Altitude, Heat, Cold and Air Pollution; EPA, Air Quality Guide for Particle Pollution

column3: A client asks to see how the hips move in a hinge. Which instructional approach directly answers the request?
column4: Demonstrate the hinge from a useful side view.
column5: AHRQ, Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Use the Teach-Back Method (Tool 5); ACSM Certification Guidebook, App. I, confidentiality Open source

column3: A client wants a spoken reminder they can use without looking up. What kind of instruction fits?
column4: A short, concrete verbal cue timed to the action.
column5: AHRQ, Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Use the Teach-Back Method (Tool 5); ACSM Certification Guidebook, App. I, confidentiality Open source

column3: A client learns the setup best by trying it. How can the trainer provide a kinesthetic learning opportunity?
column4: Offer a safe, lightly loaded practice attempt with feedback.
column5: AHRQ, Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Use the Teach-Back Method (Tool 5); ACSM Certification Guidebook, App. I, confidentiality Open source

column3: Which leg stays straight in the straight-knee wall calf stretch?
column4: The rear leg being stretched.
column5: AAOS OrthoInfo, Knee Conditioning Program, exercises 1–3, Heel Cord, Standing Quadriceps and Supine Hamstring Stretches Open source

column3: In the supine hamstring stretch, where should the client hold the raised limb while extending the knee?
column4: Behind the thigh, avoiding pressure directly on the knee.
column5: AAOS OrthoInfo, Knee Conditioning Program, exercises 1–3, Heel Cord, Standing Quadriceps and Supine Hamstring Stretches Open source

column3: During a standing knee curl, what should happen to the thigh of the working leg?
